** Preface to the First French Edition

One of us is soon to tell in all its details the story of the life of Michael Bakunin, but its general features are already sufficiently familiar. Friends and enemies know that this man was great in thought, will, persistent energy; they know also with what lofty contempt he looked down upon wealth, rank, glory, all the wretched ambitions which most human beings are base enough to entertain. A Russian gentleman related by marriage to the highest nobility of the empire, he was one of the first to enter that intrepid society of rebels who were able to release themselves from traditions, prejudices, race and class interests, and set their own comfort at naught. With them he fought the stern battle of life, aggravated by imprisonment, exile, all the dangers and all the sorrows that men of self-sacrifice have to undergo during their tormented existence.', 'The present memoir, “God and the State,” is really a fragment of a letter or report. Composed in the same manner as most of Bakunin’s other writings, it has the same literary fault, lack of proportion; moreover it breaks off abruptly: we have searched in vain to discover the end of the manuscript. Bakunin never had the time necessary to finish all the tasks he undertook. One work was not completed when others were already under way. “My life itself is a fragment,” he said to those who criticized his writings. Nevertheless, the readers of “God and the State” certainly will not regret that Bakunin’s memoir, incomplete though it be, has been published. The questions discussed in it are treated decisively and with a singular vigor of logic. Rightly addressing himself only to his honest opponents, Bakunin demonstrates to them the emptiness of their belief in that divine authority on which all temporal authorities are founded; he proves to them the purely human genesis of all governments; finally, without stopping to discuss those bases of the State already condemned by public morality, such as physical superiority, violence, nobility, wealth, he does justice to the theory which would entrust science with the government of societies. Supposing even that it were possible to recognize, amid the conflict of rival ambitions and intrigues, who are the pretenders and who are the real savants, and that a method of election could be found which would not fail to lodge the power in the hands of those whose knowledge is authentic, what guarantee could they offer us of the wisdom and honesty of their government? On the contrary, can we not foresee in these new masters the same follies and the same crimes found in those of former days and of the present time? In the first place, science is not: it is becoming. The learned man of to-day is but the know-nothing of tomorrow', 'But we may reassure ourselves: all these academicians will not have the audacity of Alexander in cutting with his sword the Gordian knot; they will not lift the blade of Charlemagne. Government by science is becoming as impossible as that of divine right, wealth, or brute force. All powers are henceforth to be submitted to pitiless criticism. Men in whom the sentiment of equality is born suffer themselves no longer to be governed; they learn to govern themselves. In precipitating from the heights of the heavens him from whom all power is reputed to descend, societies unseat also all those who reigned in his name. Such is the revolution now in progress. States are breaking up to give place to a new order, in which, as Bakunin was fond of saying, “human justice will be substituted for divine justice.” If it is allowable to cite any one name from those of the revolutionists who have taken part in this immense work of renovation, there is not one that may be singled out with more justice than that of Michael Bakunin.

reference: In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Marx defines self-estrangement as the process wherein the worker's own labor activity becomes an alien force turned against him, reducing his personal life energy to suffering and powerlessness. In God and the State, Bakunin formulates a psychological law of privilege, asserting that any privileged position—whether political or economic—depraves the mind and heart of the privileged individual. While Marx focuses on how compulsory labor alienates the worker from his own productive activity, Bakunin emphasizes how holding systemic privilege morally and intellectually corrupts the ruling classes.

Karl Marx and Mikhail Bakunin had fundamentally different perspectives on social revolution, which are reflected in their respective works "A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy" and "Appeal to the Slavs."

### Karl Marx's Perspective in "A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy"

1. **Economic Determinism**: Marx believed that economic relations and class struggles were the primary drivers of historical change. He argued that the mode of production (the way in which society produces its means of subsistence) shapes the social, political, and ideological structures of society. In "A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy," Marx emphasizes the importance of material production and the economic base of society.

2. **Class Struggle**: Marx saw the proletariat (the working class) as the revolutionary class that would overthrow the capitalist system. He believed that the proletariat would seize control of the means of production and establish a classless society through a proletarian revolution. This revolution would be a result of the inherent contradictions within capitalism, such as the alienation of workers from their labor and the exploitation of the working class by the bourgeoisie.

3. **State and Revolution**: Marx's view of the state is that it is an instrument of class rule. He believed that the state would wither away after the revolution, as class distinctions disappear. In "A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy," Marx does not explicitly discuss the state's role in the revolutionary process, but his later works, such as "The Civil War in France," do address this.

### Mikhail Bakunin's Perspective in "Appeal to the Slavs"

1. **Anti-State and Anti-Hierarchical**: Bakunin was a strong advocate for the abolition of the state and all forms of hierarchical authority. He believed that the state was inherently oppressive and that true freedom could only be achieved through the destruction of the state and the establishment of a decentralized, voluntary association of individuals. In "Appeal to the Slavs," Bakunin calls for the dissolution of existing states and the creation of a free federation of Slavic nations.

2. **Revolutionary Anarchism**: Bakunin's vision of revolution was based on the spontaneous actions of the masses, rather than the organized efforts of a vanguard party. He believed that the working class and other oppressed groups would rise up in a general strike or insurrection, overthrowing the existing order. Bakunin's revolutionary anarchism emphasizes the importance of direct action, mutual aid, and the self-organization of the people.

3. **Nationalism and Solidarity**: In "Appeal to the Slavs," Bakunin appeals to the Slavic nations to unite and fight against their common oppressors, particularly the Russian Empire. He sees the liberation of the Slavic peoples as a key step towards the broader liberation of all humanity. Bakunin's revolutionary vision is rooted in the idea of national liberation and the solidarity of oppressed peoples.

### Key Differences

1. **Role of the State**: Marx sees the state as an instrument of class rule that will eventually wither away, while Bakunin calls for its complete abolition.

2. **Class vs. Nationalism**: Marx focuses on class struggle and the proletariat, while Bakunin emphasizes national liberation and the solidarity of oppressed peoples.

3. **Organized vs. Spontaneous Revolution**: Marx envisions a revolution led by a vanguard party, while Bakunin advocates for a spontaneous uprising driven by the masses.

4. **Economic vs. Political Focus**: Marx's analysis is primarily economic, while Bakunin's is more political and focuses on the state and its institutions.

In summary, while both Marx and Bakunin advocate for social revolution, their approaches differ significantly in terms of the role of the state, the nature of the revolutionary process, and the primary drivers of historical change.

In Appeal to the Slavs, Bakunin attributes the 1848 revolutionary movements to the spontaneous instinct of the popular masses, who simultaneously raised the national and social questions of freedom. While Marx grounds revolutionary eras in structural, economic contradictions between productive forces and property relations, Bakunin attributes revolutionary outbreaks to the immediate, intuitive drives of the working masses.

Introduction
The overall theme of

is the relationship between the conscious revolutionary vanguard, Bakunin’s Alliance, and the working masses in and out of the International whom it is trying to influence in a revolutionary direction, how to organize the unorganized and how to radicalize them when they are organized is the main theme though Bakunin digresses to other matters not strictly related to it. The Program of the Alliance
opens with a discussion of union bureaucracy, a description of how the executive committees elected by the sections of rank-and-file local unions tend to become transformed from being the intended agents to the masters of the membership. He stresses that no organization, however free, can long withstand the lethargy and indifference of the membership without degenerating into some form of dictatorship.

Bakunin’s “Fabrica sections” were composed of native citizens, the highly skilled, better-paid watchmakers and jewelry workers, most of whom favored parliamentary action and class collaboration. and gross that it might appear impossible for any person of candour and

Mikhail Bakunin's rejection of religious morality in "God and the State" and John Stuart Mill's advocacy of utilitarian morality in "Utilitarianism" can be compared as follows:

1. **Bakunin's Rejection of Religious Morality:**
   - Bakunin argues against the idea of a divine authority and the concept of a "divine justice" that supersedes human justice. He suggests that the belief in a divine authority is a tool used by those in power to maintain control over the masses.
   - Bakunin emphasizes that all forms of power, including those derived from religion, are subject to critical examination and should be dismantled. He believes that human justice should replace divine justice.
   - Bakunin's view is rooted in a materialist perspective, where he sees ideas and beliefs as products of material conditions and social structures.

2. **Mill's Utilitarian Morality:**
   - Mill advocates for a form of utilitarianism, which he defines as the principle that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness.
   - Mill argues that the ultimate criterion for morality is the greatest happiness for the greatest number. He believes that moral rules and principles should be judged based on their utility in promoting overall happiness.
   - Mill's utilitarianism is more focused on the practical application of ethical principles and the consequences of actions, rather than on abstract theological or metaphysical arguments.

3. **Key Differences:**
   - **Source of Morality:** Bakunin rejects the idea of divine or religious authority as a source of morality, while Mill sees utility as a practical and empirical basis for moral judgments.
   - **Scope of Application:** Bakunin's critique is more focused on the political and social structures that derive from religious authority, whereas Mill's utilitarianism is a broader ethical framework applicable to individual and collective actions.
   - **Methodology:** Bakunin's approach is more revolutionary and calls for the overthrow of existing power structures, while Mill's utilitarianism is more about reforming and improving existing social and moral practices.

In summary, while both Bakunin and Mill reject traditional religious justifications for morality, they do so for different reasons and propose different methods for establishing a new moral order. Bakunin's rejection is more radical and calls for the dismantling of all forms of authority, whereas Mill's utilitarianism seeks to reform and improve society through practical ethical considerations.

John Stuart Mill's and Mikhail Bakunin's views on contractual moral obligations and social contract theory present stark contrasts, reflecting their different philosophical and political perspectives.

### John Stuart Mill's View in "On Liberty"

In "On Liberty," Mill frames the concept of individual liberty and the limits of state intervention through a utilitarian lens. He argues that individuals have a right to freedom as long as their actions do not harm others. Mill's approach is based on the principle that individuals should be free to pursue their own happiness and development, provided they do not infringe upon the equal rights of others. This is encapsulated in his famous statement: "the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others."

Mill's view on contractual obligations is more nuanced. He acknowledges that social contracts can be useful in establishing a framework for mutual respect and cooperation, but he emphasizes that these contracts should be based on mutual agreement and should not infringe on individual freedoms. For Mill, the social contract is a means to an end—promoting the greatest happiness for the greatest number—rather than an end in itself.

### Mikhail Bakunin's Rejection in "Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism"

Mikhail Bakunin, on the other hand, vehemently rejects the social contract theory, viewing it as a tool of oppression and a means by which the powerful impose their will on the masses. In his essay "Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism," Bakunin argues that the social contract is inherently flawed because it is based on the idea that individuals consent to be governed, which he sees as a farce. He writes:

> "The social contract is a lie, a fraud, a swindle. It is a deception practiced on the people by the ruling classes, who have always governed, and who have always used the social contract as a means of perpetuating their power."

Bakunin believes that the social contract is a mechanism by which the ruling classes maintain their dominance over the working class. He argues that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of all forms of hierarchical and authoritarian structures, including the state. Instead of a social contract, Bakunin advocates for a decentralized, federative organization of society based on mutual aid and voluntary association.

### Key Differences

1. **Purpose of the Social Contract:**
   - **Mill:** Sees the social contract as a means to promote individual freedom and happiness, within the bounds of not harming others.
   - **Bakunin:** Views the social contract as a tool of oppression and a means to perpetuate the power of the ruling classes.

2. **Role of the State:**
   - **Mill:** Advocates for a limited state that protects individual rights and promotes the general welfare.
   - **Bakunin:** Seeks the abolition of the state and the establishment of a decentralized, voluntary association of individuals.

3. **Nature of Obligations:**
   - **Mill:** Emphasizes mutual obligations and agreements that respect individual freedoms.
   - **Bakunin:** Rejects any form of obligation that is imposed by a hierarchical structure, advocating for voluntary and egalitarian associations.

In summary, while Mill sees the social contract as a useful framework for mutual respect and cooperation, Bakunin views it as a deceptive and oppressive mechanism that must be dismantled. Their differing perspectives reflect their broader philosophical and political ideologies, with Mill advocating for a more moderate reformist approach and Bakunin calling for a radical transformation of society.

He feared that an immediate massive expropriation might find the workers unprepared to take control. This would leave the way open for a bureaucratic administrative apparatus. It would lead to a worse evil, namely, the restoration of authoritarian institutions. The fact that Bakunin called for the destruction of all oppressive institutions does not mean that he favored premature changes in certain areas. However, some years later he included expropriation in his program when the workers demanded it.

In touching on the constructive potentialities of cooperative workers’ associations, Bakunin speculated that in the future mankind would not be politically organized into nations. National frontiers would be abolished. Human society would be organized industrially according to the needs of production. In view of the existing situation, it was not a matter of immediate concern and he merely mentioned it in passing. Later on, this idea occupied a key place in Bakunin’s anarcho-syndicalist program for the International.

To avoid misunderstanding, the reader should know that before anarchism became an organized movement, Bakunin and the anarchists in general used the term “State” and allied expressions in a twofold sense: with reference to the social collectivity or social order, and as designating the complex of repressive institutions exercising intrusive political authority over society and the individual. This approach involves a compromise with existing political structures and a belief that political liberty must precede economic liberty.

Thus, while Marxian socialists advocate for a temporary state to facilitate economic liberation, anarchists like Bakunin reject the use of any political power, viewing it as inherently oppressive and counterproductive to the goal of true liberation.

Bakunin's organizational vision in "Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism" contrasts with Marx and Engels' program in the Manifesto of the Communist Party in several key ways:

1. **Federalism vs. Centralized State**: Bakunin advocates for federalism, emphasizing a decentralized, confederal structure where power is distributed among local communities and regions. He views the state as an oppressive institution and prefers a system where the state's role is minimized. In contrast, Marx and Engels propose a centralized state under the dictatorship of the proletariat, which would eventually wither away but would initially serve as a tool to suppress the bourgeoisie.

2. **Anarchism vs. Authoritarianism**: Bakunin explicitly calls himself an anarchist, rejecting any form of hierarchical authority, including the state. He believes in the spontaneous organization of free associations based on individual and collective liberty. Marx and Engels, while critical of the existing state, do not explicitly advocate for the abolition of the state. They see the state as a necessary transitional phase to be replaced by a stateless society.

3. **Economic Regulation**: Bakunin opposes state regulation of the economy, favoring a system where economic relations are governed by the laws of social economy, discovered through the collective action of free associations. Marx and Engels, on the other hand, support the idea of state control over the economy to ensure the transition to a classless society.

4. **Role of the Proletariat**: Bakunin emphasizes the role of the working class in overthrowing the existing order but does not see them as a vanguard leading the revolution. He believes in the spontaneous uprising of the masses. Marx and Engels, however, see the proletariat as the revolutionary class that will lead the struggle against capitalism and establish a dictatorship of the proletariat.

5. **Internationalism**: Bakunin advocates for an international confederation of free states and regions, focusing on solidarity and cooperation among nations. Marx and Engels, while international in their outlook, propose a unified state that would eventually dissolve into a stateless society.

6. **Critique of Religion and State**: Bakunin's critique of the state and religion is more radical, seeing them as tools of oppression. He calls for the complete abolition of both. Marx and Engels, while critical of religion, do not advocate for its complete abolition, seeing it as a reflection of class relations.

These differences highlight the fundamental contrast between Bakunin's anarchist vision and Marx and Engels' more statist and revolutionary approach as outlined in the Manifesto.
reference: In Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism, Bakunin demands that society and collective property be organized strictly from below upward through free association, rejecting all top-down authority as slavery. Conversely, Marx and Engels outline a program in the Manifesto of the Communist Party where the proletariat uses its political supremacy to centralize all instruments of production in the hands of the state, organized as the ruling class. While Bakunin insists on decentralized, voluntary federation from below without state power, Marx and Engels advocate using centralized state power to expropriate capital and control production.

Here's a comparison of the two perspectives:

### Mikhail Bakunin's Perspective on State Security

1. **Critique of the State**: Bakunin was a fierce critic of the state, viewing it as an instrument of oppression and a means of maintaining class domination. He believed that the state inherently serves the interests of the ruling class and is a barrier to true freedom and equality.

2. **Anarchism**: Bakunin advocated for a form of anarchism, which seeks to abolish the state entirely. He believed that the state is a tool of the few to control the many and that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of the state.

3. **Security and Freedom**: Bakunin argued that security and freedom are not mutually exclusive but are in fact contradictory. He believed that the state's security measures are inherently oppressive and that true security can only be achieved through the collective self-organization of the people.

4. **Mutual Aid**: Bakunin emphasized the importance of mutual aid and cooperation among individuals and communities. He believed that social bonds and mutual aid could provide the necessary security and stability without the need for a coercive state.

### John Stuart Mill's Perspective on Equal Social Relations

1. **Utilitarianism**: Mill's utilitarianism posits that the rightness of an action is determined by its consequences, specifically by the amount of happiness or utility it produces. He believed that the state should aim to maximize overall happiness.

2. **Equal Social Relations**: Mill advocated for equal social relations, particularly in his work "Utilitarianism." He argued that the state should promote equal opportunities and fair treatment for all individuals, ensuring that no one is unfairly disadvantaged.

3. **Liberalism and Individual Rights**: While Mill did not advocate for the complete abolition of the state, he did support a limited state that protects individual rights and promotes social welfare. He believed that the state should intervene to correct inequalities and ensure that the happiness of the majority is not compromised by the actions of the few.

4. **Social Justice**: Mill's utilitarianism includes a strong emphasis on social justice. He argued that the state should work to create a society where the happiness of all individuals is considered, and that inequalities should be addressed to ensure that the least advantaged are not left behind.

### Comparison

1. **Role of the State**: 
   - **Bakunin**: Sees the state as an oppressive institution that should be abolished.
   - **Mill**: Sees the state as a necessary institution that should be limited but still exist to promote the greatest happiness.

2. **Social Relations**:
   - **Bakunin**: Emphasizes mutual aid and collective self-organization as the basis for social relations.
   - **Mill**: Advocates for equal social relations and the state's role in promoting fairness and justice.

3. **Security**:
   - **Bakunin**: Sees security as a product of mutual aid and collective self-organization, not the state.
   - **Mill**: Sees security as a product of a limited state that protects individual rights and promotes social welfare.

4. **Philosophical Foundations**:
   - **Bakunin**: Grounded in anarchism and a critique of state power.
   - **Mill**: Grounded in utilitarianism and a belief in the state's role in promoting the greatest happiness.

In summary, while both thinkers advocate for a more equitable society, they differ significantly in their views on the role of the state and the means by which social relations can be improved. Bakunin sees the state as an obstacle to freedom and equality, while Mill sees it as a necessary but limited institution that can help achieve these goals.

Mikhail Bakunin's concept of revolutionary organization, as outlined in "The Program of the International Brotherhood," contrasts significantly with Marx and Engels' central objective in the Manifesto of the Communist Party. Here are some key differences:

### Bakunin's Vision:
1. **Anti-Authoritarianism**: Bakunin was a strong advocate for anti-authoritarianism and opposed the idea of a centralized, hierarchical organization. He believed that the International should be a loose federation of autonomous groups, rather than a centralized body with a rigid structure.
2. **Direct Action**: Bakunin emphasized direct action and spontaneous uprisings as the primary means of achieving revolution. He believed that the working class should organize through mutual aid and self-organization, rather than through a structured political party.
3. **Decentralization**: Bakunin's vision was decentralized, with a focus on local and regional autonomy. He saw the International as a network of independent groups that could coordinate and support each other, but not as a top-down organization.
4. **Immediate Action**: Bakunin was more focused on immediate action and practical, day-to-day struggles. He believed that the International should be involved in immediate, concrete actions to improve the lives of workers, rather than waiting for a theoretical revolution.
5. **Anti-Statism**: Bakunin was deeply opposed to the state and believed that the state was inherently oppressive. He saw the state as an instrument of the ruling class and sought to dismantle it through revolutionary means.

### Marx and Engels' Vision:
1. **Centralized Organization**: Marx and Engels envisioned a more centralized and structured organization. They believed that a strong, unified party was necessary to guide the working class towards revolution.
2. **Theoretical Foundation**: Marx and Engels emphasized the importance of a theoretical foundation for the working class. They believed that the International should focus on spreading Marxist ideas and educating the working class about the nature of capitalism and the need for revolution.
3. **Political Action**: Marx and Engels were more focused on political action and the use of the state to achieve their goals. They believed that the International should work within the existing political system to gain power and influence.
4. **Long-Term Strategy**: Marx and Engels were more focused on a long-term strategy for revolution. They believed that the International should be patient and work towards building a strong, organized working class that could eventually overthrow the capitalist system.
5. **State Power**: Marx and Engels were not opposed to the idea of the state, but they believed that the state could be transformed into a tool for the working class. They saw the state as a potential ally in the struggle for socialism.

### Key Differences:
- **Structure**: Bakunin's organization was decentralized and anti-hierarchical, while Marx and Engels envisioned a more centralized and structured party.
- **Means of Action**: Bakunin emphasized direct action and immediate struggle, while Marx and Engels focused on theoretical education and political action.
- **Role of the State**: Bakunin was anti-statist, while Marx and Engels saw the state as a potential tool for the working class.
- **Immediate vs. Long-Term Goals**: Bakunin was more focused on immediate action and practical struggles, while Marx and Engels were more focused on long-term strategy and theoretical education.

In summary, Bakunin's vision of revolutionary organization was more decentralized, anti-authoritarian, and focused on immediate action, while Marx and Engels' vision was more centralized, theoretical, and focused on long-term political strategy.
reference: In The Program of the International Brotherhood, Bakunin emphasizes that revolutions arise spontaneously from circumstances rather than being made by individuals, requiring only a secret association of 'International Brothers' to serve as a non-dictatorial organ within popular anarchy. In the Manifesto of the Communist Party, Marx and Engels define the core objective of Communism as the explicit abolition of bourgeois private property, which they identify as the ultimate system of class exploitation. While Bakunin focuses on organizing an informal, non-directive vanguard to assist spontaneous popular anarchy, Marx and Engels frame revolutionary purpose around the systematic economic destruction of bourgeois property relations.

necessary evil,

Such is the theory, but in practice these same doctrinaire liberals, when the existence or the stability of the State is seriously threatened, are just as fanatical defenders of the State as are the monarchists and the Jacobins.', 'Man completely realizes his individual freedom as well as his personality only through the individuals who surround him, and thanks only to the labor and the collective power of society. Without society he would surely remain the most stupid and the most miserable among all the other ferocious beasts.... Society, far from decreasing his freedom, on the contrary creates the individual freedom of all human beings. Society is the root, the tree, and liberty is its fruit. Hence, in every epoch, man must seek his freedom not at the beginning but at the end of history. It can be said that the real and complete emancipation of every individual is the true, the great, the supreme aim of history....

The materialistic. realistic, and collectivist conception of freedom, as opposed to the idealistic, is this: Man becomes conscious of himself and his humanity only in society and only by the collective action of the whole society. He frees himself from the yoke of external nature only by collective and social labor, which alone can transform the earth into an abode favorable to the development of humanity. Without such material emancipation the intellectual and moral emancipation of the individual is impossible. He can emancipate himself from the yoke of his own nature, i.e. subordinate his instincts and the movements of his body to the conscious direction of his mind, the development of which is fostered only by education and training. But education and training are preeminently and exclusively social ... hence the isolated individual cannot possibly become conscious of his freedom.

To be free ... means to be acknowledged and treated as such by all his fellowmen. The liberty of every individual is only the reflection of his own humanity, or his human right through the conscience of all free men, his brothers and his equals.', 'I am truly free only when all human beings, men and women, are equally free. The freedom of other men, far from negating or limiting my freedom, is, on the contrary, its necessary premise and confirmation. It is the slavery of other men that sets up a barrier to my freedom, or what amounts to the same thing, it is their bestiality which is the negation of my humanity. For my dignity as a man, my human right which consists of refusing to obey any other man, and to determine my own acts in conformity with my convictions is reflected by the equally free conscience of all and confirmed by the consent of all humanity. My personal freedom, confirmed by the liberty of all, extends to infinity.

The materialistic conception of freedom is therefore a very positive, very complex thing, and above all, eminently social, because it can be realized only in society and by the strictest equality and solidarity among all men. It is the fullest development of all the faculties and powers of every human being, by education, by scientific training, and by material prosperity; things which can only be provided for every individual by the collective, material, intellectual, manual, and sedentary labor of society in general.

John Stuart Mill emphasizes individual self-determination as a fundamental aspect of liberty. He argues that individuals have inherent rights that should not be infringed upon by society, and that true freedom is achieved when individuals are not coerced by others, including the state. Mill believes that individuals are naturally prior to the state and that their liberties are not forfeited when they form a social contract.

In contrast, Mikhail Bakunin views freedom as a collective and social phenomenon. He argues that individual freedom is realized through the collective power of society and that the true freedom of an individual is confirmed by the freedom of all. Bakunin sees the state as an obstacle to individual freedom and believes that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of the state and the establishment of a free association of individuals.

Bakunin's view is that individual freedom is not something that exists independently of society but is dependent on the collective freedom of all. He sees the state as a tool of oppression that limits individual freedom, and thus, the goal should be the complete abolition of the state to achieve true freedom for all individuals. Mill, on the other hand, acknowledges the importance of society but maintains that individuals have inherent rights that should be protected from the state and other individuals.
reference: In On Liberty, Mill stresses individual self-determination, warning that letting others choose one's life plan reduces human action to mere ape-like imitation rather than full faculty development. In Man, Society, and Freedom, Bakunin maintains that human consciousness and individual freedom are not solitary facts, but collective products generated through social action. While Mill focuses on shielding individual self-choice from social pressure, Bakunin emphasizes that individual personality and freedom can only emerge through collective social existence.
